title: Why does a bigger rear gear make hills easier?
question: Why does shifting to a bigger rear gear make a hill feel easier, when your legs are just as strong as before?
audience: Curious teenagers and adults anywhere who ride a bike and have shifted gears on a hill. They know gears from machines and clocks, and many have heard the word 'torque' from car or motorbike specs, but they have never seen why a small gear driving a big one turns it more strongly.
promise: A small gear driving a big one trades speed for torque: with three times the teeth, the big gear turns three times slower but with three times the torque, and that is why a bigger rear gear makes a hill easier, at the price of more pedal turns.

loop.line: That's why / a bigger rear gear makes a hill feel easy.

It thins under the gear mechanism (s04 to s08) and opens on the bicycle and the recap. Every shot starts on a beat. Effects per shot are in each shot's 'sound': soft pen and ruler strokes as lines draw on (the template's own), a compass squeak for circles, a quiet tooth click per tooth in s04 and s05, one soft ping on each '×3' (s08 and s13, the same idea), a light chain rattle in s10 and s12, freewheel ticks in s14 and s15. facts.claim: Meshing gears pass their teeth one for one, so the driven gear turns (teeth of the driver ÷ teeth of the driven) times for each turn of the driver; two external gears turn in opposite directions. The film's s04 numbers three teeth as they pass and s05 turns the gears opposite ways.
facts.source: Bureau of Naval Personnel, Basic Machines (NAVPERS 10624, 1946), ch. 6 'Gears', pp. 71-73: 'Wheel A has 10 teeth which mesh with the 40 teeth on wheel B. Wheel A will have to rotate four times to cause B to make one revolution'; 'When two external gears mesh, they rotate in opposite directions' (archive.org/details/BasicMachines10624). Also Shigley & Mischke, Mechanical Engineering Design, ch. 13 (via Wikipedia, 'Gear train').

facts.claim: The film's pair: 12 teeth driving 36. Ratio 36 ÷ 12 = 3. One turn of the 12-tooth gear moves 12 teeth past the mesh, which is 12/36 = 1/3 of a turn of the big gear = 120°. On screen: '12', '36', '1 TURN · 360°', '1/3 TURN · 120°', 'a third'.

At the pitch point the tooth of each gear pushes the other with the same force F (action and reaction). Torque is force times the distance from the axle, so the small gear's torque is F × 18 mm and the big gear's F × 54 mm: three times as much. This is the gear's mechanical advantage, teeth of the driven ÷ teeth of the driver = 36/12 = 3 (ideal, with no losses). On screen: 'r 18', 'r 54', '54 ÷ 18 = 3', 'TORQUE ×3'. Simplification: the tooth force really acts along the line of action at the 20° pressure angle; the arrows show its tangential part, which is the part that turns the gear; friction losses (small for spur gears) are left out.
facts.source: Basic Machines (1946), ch. 6, 'Magnifying force with gears', p. 74: 'M.A. (theoretical) = To/Ta, in which To = number of teeth on driven gear; Ta = number of teeth on driver gear', and 'wherever there is a speed reduction, the effect of the effort you apply is multiplied'; Wikipedia, 'Gear train', 'Torque ratio analysis using virtual work' and 'Mechanical advantage' (MA = N_B / N_A).

facts.claim: The pair's dimensions, spur gears of module m = 3 mm, 20° pressure angle: pitch diameter d = z × m = 36 mm (12 teeth) and 108 mm (36 teeth), so pitch radii 18 and 54 mm; centre distance (12 + 36) × 3 / 2 = 72 mm. The 12-tooth pinion is profile-shifted by x = +0.6 so it is not undercut (KHK's own 12-tooth example uses x = +0.6) and the 36-tooth wheel by x = −0.6, so the shifts cancel and the centre distance and pitch circles stay as above; tip diameters d + 2m(1 + x) = 45.6 and 110.4 mm, root diameters d − 2.5m + 2xm = 32.1 and 96.9 mm. Drawn at 6 px per mm (sheet scale 1:1). On screen: 'Ø108 · 36 TEETH', 'Ø36 · 12 TEETH', 'm 3', and the gear data table (z 36 and 12, m 3, α 20°, x −0.6 and +0.6). The teeth are true involutes generated by one basic rack (flanks at 20°, cutter tip 1.25 m with a 0.38 m tip radius, so each root has its fillet) with 0.1 m of backlash, so the flanks touch and never cross. Section A–A's face width (30 mm), hub (Ø60 mm, 20 mm proud) and bore (Ø25 mm, keyway 8 × 3.3 mm, DIN 6885) are proportions chosen for a stock gear of this size and are not stated on screen.
facts.source: KHK Gears, Gear Technical Reference, 'Calculation of Gear Dimensions', 4.1 Spur gears, Table 4.1 (reference diameter d = zm, addendum 1.00m, tooth depth 2.25m) and the profile-shifted spur gear table (tip diameter d + 2m(1 + x), root diameter d − 2.5m + 2xm; its worked example has 12 teeth and x = +0.6) (khkgears.net).

facts.claim: A gear pair exchanges speed for torque: what the driven gear gains in torque it loses in speed (1/3 the speed × 3 times the torque = the same power, minus friction). On screen: 'Speed is traded for torque', 'TURNS 1/3', 'TORQUE ×3', 'TRADED'.
facts.source: University of Florida, EML2322L Design and Manufacturing Lab, 'Gears and gearing': 'The primary purpose of gears is to exchange speed for torque or vice-versa' (web.mae.ufl.edu/designlab); Wikipedia, 'Gear train' (virtual work: torque ratio = speed ratio).

facts.claim: Bicycle chain has a 1/2-inch (12.7 mm) pitch (ANSI #40, ISO 606 #08). A sprocket's pitch diameter is p / sin(180°/N): 11 teeth Ø45.08 mm, 33 teeth Ø133.61 mm, 32 teeth Ø129.57 mm, 51 teeth Ø206.30 mm. Pitch radii 22.54 and 66.80 mm (on screen 'Ø45.1', 'Ø133.6', 'r 22.5', 'r 66.8'); 66.80 / 22.54 = 2.96.
facts.source: Wikipedia, 'Bicycle chain', section Pitch (1/2 in, ANSI #40, ISO 606 #8); sprocket pitch diameter formula PD = P / sin(180°/N) per ASME B29.1 as given by Engineers Edge, 'Sprocket Pitch Diameter' and the Autodesk Inventor help 'Geometry Design Properties of Roller Chains' (read through search summaries; the formula's page is an image). Arithmetic in storyboard.build.py.

facts.claim: The real drivetrain drawn: Shimano Deore CS-M5100 11-speed cassette, 11-51 teeth, sprockets 11-13-15-18-21-24-28-33-39-45-51; Shimano Deore FC-M5100-1 crankset, 32-tooth chainring, 175 mm cranks (also made with 30 teeth and 170 mm). This group is fitted, for example, to the Polygon Xtrada 6 (2024). On screen: '11 TEETH', '33 TEETH', 'FRONT CHAINRING 32', 'CASSETTE 11–51 TEETH'.
facts.source: Shimano product pages for CS-M5100-11 and FC-M5100-1 (bike.shimano.com, via search); sprocket list from SJS Cycles and bike-components.de listings of the CS-M5100 11-51T; chainring and crank options from Halfords and Competitive Cyclist listings; Xtrada 6 (2024) spec via bikesonline.com (search summary). The Shimano pages themselves refused a direct fetch (403).

facts.claim: The bike drawn is the side elevation of a Polygon Xtrada 7 (2021), size XL, 29 in: chainstay 435 mm (430.1 horizontal), bottom-bracket drop 65 mm, wheelbase 1191 mm, stack 637, reach 470, seat tube 500 mm c-t, head angle 67°, seat angle 75°, head tube 105 mm, fork offset 44.3 mm, tyre 29 × 2.25 in (outer Ø736.3 mm), cranks 175 mm. Simplifications: the saddle height (760 mm from the bottom bracket), stem and bar are drawn for a rider of the size, the rear derailleur is drawn as its two pulleys only, and the hill is a 6° slope chosen for the picture (no grade is stated on screen). The cassette and chainring of f7 are drawn on this frame.
facts.source: bikeinsights.com, '2021 Polygon Bikes Xtrada 7 XL 29"' geometry (fetched). The same chainstay figures appear for the Xtrada 6 (2024) in its listing (search summary).

facts.claim: With the same chainring and the same push on the pedals, the chain's pull is the same whichever rear sprocket it is on (pull = crank torque ÷ chainring pitch radius). The rear sprocket is fixed to the wheel while pedalling, so the torque at the wheel is that pull × the sprocket's pitch radius: 66.80 / 22.54 = 2.96 times as much on the 33 as on the 11; averaged over a turn it is exactly 33/11 = 3 (the work done per pedal turn is the same). On screen: 'The chain pulls the same', 'The 33 gives the wheel 3 times the torque', 'TORQUE ×3'. Losses in the chain are left out.
facts.source: Basic Machines (1946), ch. 3 'The wheel and axle', p. 33: 'When you are pedaling, the sprocket is fixed to the wheel, so the combination is a true wheel-and-axle machine'; torque = force × radius and MA = teeth ratio as in f3; Wikipedia, 'Gear train' ('The speed ratios of chain and belt drives are computed in the same way as gear ratios'). Arithmetic in storyboard.build.py.

facts.claim: Distance per pedal turn: the chain moves 32 teeth per crank turn, so the wheel turns 32/11 = 2.91 times on the 11 and 32/33 = 0.97 times on the 33. The tyre's circumference is π × 736.3 = 2313 mm, so one pedal turn moves the bike 6.73 m on the 11 and 2.24 m on the 33: three times the pedal turns for the same distance. On screen: '6.7 m', '2.2 m', '1 PEDAL TURN'.
facts.source: Arithmetic from f7 and f8 (tyre outer diameter 736.3 mm from bikeinsights.com), shown in storyboard.build.py; rolling without slip.

facts.claim: Why the hill feels lighter: climbing needs a certain force at the tyre; on the bigger sprocket the same push on the pedal gives about three times the turning force at the wheel (f9), so a third of the push does the same job, at a third of the distance per pedal turn (f10). On screen: 'A bigger rear gear makes a hill feel easy', 'Slower, but much easier', 'SAME PUSH'.
facts.source: Follows from f9 and f10; the trade of speed for torque is f5 (UF EML2322L).

shots.caption: The chain pulls *the same*.
shots.teaches: With the same chainring and the same push on the pedal, the chain pulls with the same force whichever sprocket it is on.
shots.screen: Sheet 4, two side views on one base line: the 11-tooth sprocket centred at (330, 560) and the 33-tooth at (1150, 560), both in yellow at 3.2 px per mm, each with the chain over its top (plates as two thin lines, rollers as small circles every 12.7 mm) running off to the right towards the chainring. On each chain run an arrow 'F' of the same length pulling right.
shots.motion: The chains settle onto the teeth (rollers drop into the gaps); both arrows draw out together and stop at the same length.
shots.carries: The two sprockets with their chains and arrows.
shots.transition: Radius dimensions draw from the centres up to the chain line.
shots.sound: A soft chain clink as each chain seats; one ruler slide for both arrows.
shots.check: The two F arrows are identical in length and height above their axles' chain line.

frames.note: The two sprockets apart; the chains drop onto them.
The same F on both chains.

shots.caption: The 33 gives the wheel *3 times* the torque.
shots.teaches: Same pull, three times the radius: the 33-tooth sprocket turns the wheel with about three times the torque of the 11.
shots.screen: Sheet 4 as s12, with vertical radius dimensions from each axle to its chain line: 'r 22.5' and 'r 66.8' (mm). In the free space under the arrows, two outline bars: 'F × 22.5' and 'F × 66.8', the second three times the first, '×3' in yellow.
shots.motion: The radius dimensions draw up from the axles; the bars draw up from one base line, the second to three times the first's height; '×3' is written on the beat.
shots.transition: The sprockets roll away along the base line, which becomes a road.
shots.sound: Two ruler ticks; the same soft ping as s08 on '×3' (it is the same idea).
shots.check: r 22.5 and r 66.8 are written; the bars stand 1 : 3 (the ideal ratio, 33/11; the radii give 2.96).

frames.note: Radius dimensions draw up from both axles.

draw.text: THE 33 GIVES THE WHEEL 3 TIMES THE TORQUE.

shots.caption: The price: one pedal turn moves you only *2.2 m*.
shots.teaches: The price: on the 33 one pedal turn moves the bike 2.2 m, on the 11 it moves 6.7 m; three times the turns for the same distance.
shots.screen: Sheet 5 'DISTANCE PER PEDAL TURN', two roads drawn as base lines across the sheet at 1 mm = 0.223 px. Top, 'COG 11': the wheel (Ø736 mm = 164 px) rolls from x 180 to x 1680, ticks at each full wheel turn (2.9 turns), dimension '6.7 m'. Bottom, 'COG 33': the same wheel rolls only to x 680 (0.97 turn), dimension '2.2 m' in yellow. Both start on one dashed start line.
shots.motion: One pedal turn, the same 2.4 s for both: the top wheel rolls three times as far as the bottom one in the same time, each leaving its tick marks; the dimension lines draw behind them; the values are written as they stop.
shots.carries: The bottom road with its yellow 2.2 m.
shots.transition: The sheet tilts up to the hill of s01 as the bike is drawn back on it.
shots.sound: A freewheel tick under each rolling wheel (the top one ticks three times as often).
shots.check: 6.73 m and 2.24 m are drawn as 1500 and 500 px: 3 : 1. The wheel's circumference is 516 px.

frames.note: Both wheels on the dashed start line.

shots.caption: Slower, but much *easier*.
shots.teaches: The payoff on the hill: slower, but the wheel gets three times the turning force from the same push.
shots.screen: Sheet 1 again: the bike on the 6-degree hill as in s01. A curved yellow arrow round the rear wheel 'TORQUE ×3'; a small white arrow at the pedal 'SAME PUSH'; a short blue-white speed arrow along the slope 'SLOW'.
shots.motion: The bike creeps up the slope (the drawing slides along the ground line about 60 px over the shot) while the crank turns; the arrows are drawn in turn.
shots.transition: The sheet slides off to the left; the summary sheet slides in.
shots.sound: A slow freewheel-and-chain cadence; the bed lifts a little.
shots.check: The torque arrow is on the rear wheel, not the pedal; the bike is the same drawing as s01.

frames.note: The bike on the hill; the crank turns.
Arrows: TORQUE ×3 round the rear wheel, SAME PUSH at the pedal, slow along the slope.

shots.caption: Bigger rear cog: *slower, but stronger*.
shots.teaches: The answer in one sheet: a small gear driving a big one turns it slower and with more torque; on a bike that is the big rear sprocket, paid for in distance per pedal turn.
shots.screen: Sheet 'SUMMARY', three boxes across the sheet (x 100 to 1820, y 130 to 820), each a small drawing with two lines of capitals under it: (1) the 12/36 gear pair at 2.6 px per mm, '12 → 36' / '1/3 TURN · TORQUE ×3'; (2) the 11 and 33 sprockets side by side, '11 vs 33' / 'WHEEL TORQUE ×3'; (3) the two roads, 'THE PRICE' / '2.2 m PER PEDAL TURN'. The second lines in yellow.
shots.motion: The three boxes draw on left to right, one per beat; inside each the miniature redraws quickly (the same drawing as before, smaller); the lines are written; the yellow lines last.
shots.carries: The sheet, which slides back to the bike.
shots.transition: The summary sheet slides out; the hill sheet slides back into exactly the place it had at frame 0.
shots.sound: Three pen ticks rising in pitch; the bed opens up.
shots.check: Readable with the sound off; the numbers are the ones shown before (12, 36, 11, 33, 6.7 m, 2.2 m).
